Four Circle Sangaku

GeometryCirclesTriangles
What it shows: Three smaller circles sit around a triangle inside a big circle; move one point and watch their sizes change.
How to play: Drag the point C around the big circle, or focus it and use the arrow keys. Turn it with the buttons and tick hint to see the extra lines.
Look for the math

Move the point C around the circle. The three smaller circles change size, but a simple relationship between them never does. This is a sangaku, a Japanese temple geometry puzzle.

The four circles

The line AB goes straight through the middle O of the large circle, so its length is 2R. The point C lies on the circle, and D is its mirror image across AB; the chord CD is perpendicular to AB. One circle is the incircle of triangle ABC. The other two lie on the far side of AB, each touching AB and the inside of the large circle.

Where the two outer radii come from

Let d be the distance from O to CD. Joining the large circle's centre to an outer centre makes a right triangle with legs R − r and r ± d. The Pythagorean theorem gives (r ± d)² + r² = (R − r)², which solves to

rR = −(R + d) + √(2R(R + d))
rL = −(R − d) + √(2R(R − d))

The applet uses a signed distance instead: it adds +1 or −1 times K.x − O.x, where K is the foot of C on AB. That gives the same pair of radii, with left and right exchanged when C moves to the other half of the circle.

The average is the inradius

Because AB is a diameter, ABC is a right triangle with legs a = √(2R(R + d)) and b = √(2R(R − d)) and hypotenuse 2R. Its inradius is (a + b − 2R)/2. Substituting the two formulas above shows this is exactly (rR + rL)/2. The logic test checks this and both formulas at more than 1,700 positions on five circle sizes, and agrees with a second transcription of the applet's own computation at every one.

The two tangent lines

Tick Show hint: the lines through the outer centres P and Q touch the incircle, because P.x = I.x − r and Q.x = I.x + r. Their feet S and T on AB are 2r apart, and the midpoint of ST is W, exactly where the incircle touches AB. At the ends the picture degenerates: the old applet stops updating near A and divides by zero at B, so this page holds the last good diagram there.

Turn C until it is directly above O: the two outer circles become equal. Then tick hint and drag C across the top, watching the tangent lines slide with it.
